strengths: Comprehensive theoretical analysis across multiple settings (exact gradients, stochastic, distributed, momentum)
Achieves optimal convergence rates O(√Δ*L∞/√T) matching rates with known parameters
Addresses practical problem of parameter tuning in memory-efficient Sign-SGD
Provides two complementary algorithmic approaches (grid search and per-iteration adaptation)
Extensive experiments spanning logistic regression, LLaMA pre-training, and ViT fine-tuning
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: all theory assumes convex objectives but experiments use non-convex neural networks with no reconciliation
ALIAS algorithm shows worse convergence rates than non-parameter-free variant (Theorem 2 vs Remark 1: quadratically worse in Δ*, cubic in L∞), contradicting motivation
Parameter-free claim undermined: requires setting d⁰ ∈ (0,Δ*) with no guidance, lower bound f̃, initial bound γₛ, and finding τ which depends on unknown L∞
Weak experimental validation: Table 1 shows tuned baseline (2.980) outperforming ALIAS (3.017); Table 2 improvements come from momentum/Adam structure, not parameter-free mechanism
Restrictive L∞-smoothness assumption (ℓ¹-ℓ∞ smoothness) stronger than standard; natural motivation not discussed
Numerical stability concerns: denominator in λᵗ estimation can explode when step sizes are small; no analysis of this instability
Stochastic analysis limited: Theorem 3 convergence only to neighborhood; requires increasing mini-batches; complex dependence on problem-specific expectations E[1/L₀,ξ¹∞]
Missing ablations: no sensitivity analysis for d⁰, no characterization of when L∞/L₀∞ becomes problematic, no study of f̃ approximation quality effects
Insufficient baseline comparisons: limited comparison with modern parameter-free methods like Prodigy; unclear if baseline learning rates fairly tuned
Results lack error bars and significance testing; only tested on small-scale datasets; improvements over baselines are marginal

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical framework covering exact gradients, stochastic gradients, and distributed settings
Addresses a practical problem of automatic stepsize selection for Sign-SGD
Multiple algorithm variants (SOS, ALIAS, with momentum) demonstrate thorough exploration
Real-world experiments on LLaMA pretraining and ViT fine-tuning beyond toy problems
Extensive technical analysis with detailed proofs in appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: bisection procedure directly borrowed from Carmon & Hinder (2022); main contribution is application to Sign-SGD which is incremental
Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis requires knowledge of f(x*) or lower bounds, contradicting 'parameter-free' claims; initialization γₛ requires problem knowledge
Theory is not tight: Theorem 2 has extra factors (L∞/L'∞)² vs Remark 1; stochastic convergence (Theorem 3) only to neighborhood; requires increasing batch sizes (Remark 2) for deterministic rate

Weak experimental validation: marginal improvements over baselines (Tables 1-2 show ALIAS only 'slightly inferior' with differences like 3.017 vs 2.980), no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, missing key comparisons with other parameter-free methods
Computational overhead not addressed: bisection procedure requires multiple full training runs; no timing comparisons or cost analysis provided

Unclear practical utility: tuning single learning rate for Sign-SGD is simpler than proposed methods; modern practitioners prefer AdamW over Sign-SGD; LLaMA experiments use AdamW for LM head contradicting parameter-free narrative
Restrictive assumptions: L∞-smoothness with ℓ∞ norm is limiting; coordinate-wise bounded variance in stochastic setting is restrictive
Extremely dense presentation (15 pages + 54-page appendix) with overstated title 'Golden Gate'; poor motivation for why Sign-SGD is the right focus
Missing critical experiments: no ablation studies, no computational cost analysis, no visualization of learned stepsizes, only single runs without variance estimates, limited to 130M parameter LLaMA
Algorithm design issues: Algorithm 4 (Option I vs II choice unclear), Algorithm 5 (momentum variant) is ad-hoc with minimal justification, initialization step (Eq. 4) requires careful tuning of τ

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical analysis across multiple settings (exact/stochastic/distributed gradients) with formal convergence guarantees
Addresses practical problem of parameter-free optimization for expensive hyperparameter tuning in LLM training
Natural per-iteration stepsize adaptation (ALIAS) that doesn't require multiple algorithm launches unlike grid search approaches
Extends parameter-free optimization from regret minimization to function-value-based guarantees
Covers momentum-based variants and demonstrates broad applicability across convex, semi-convex, and non-convex problems
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: convex theory but non-convex experiments; stochastic theory requires increasing batch sizes but fixed batches in practice
Experimental results contradict main claims: tuned Sign-SGD with cosine schedule outperforms ALIAS in Table 1 (2.992 vs 3.017); comparison with state-of-the-art Prodigy is inconclusive

Iteration complexity in Theorem 2 Õ((Δ*)²(L∞)³/(d₀(L⁰∞)²ε²)) shows degradation vs. known-parameter case; dependence on initial approximation d₀ and local smoothness contradicts 'parameter-free' claims
ALIAS incurs 2× gradient cost per iteration (requires evaluation at ξᵗ and ξᵗ⁺¹) but no wall-clock time comparisons provided; computational overhead not addressed
Limited novelty: bisection procedure from Carmon & Hinder (2022); per-iteration adaptation is incremental; Algorithm 5 (ALIAS-Adam) lacks theoretical justification despite empirical success

Unfair experimental comparisons: different methods receive different tuning budgets, learning rate schedules, and LM Head uses AdamW for all methods; no ablation studies on key hyperparameters (d₀, f̃, λₜ sensitivity)

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical analysis across deterministic, stochastic, and distributed settings with unified treatment
Novel per-iteration adaptive stepsize mechanism using current gradient information avoids complex restart procedures
Multiple practical extensions addressing real concerns: momentum-based variant shows strong empirical results (Table 2), memory-efficient variant preserves adaptivity
Thorough experimental validation with detailed ablation studies (Tables 5-6, gradient noise robustness) across LLaMA and ViT models
Extensive appendices with proofs and supplementary experiments demonstrate technical rigor and reproducibility
Clear motivation and positioning relative to prior work in parameter-free optimization literature
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: all convergence analysis assumes convex smooth objectives (Assumptions 3.1-3.2) while applications are non-convex neural networks; convergence to gradient norm is weaker in non-convex regime

Suboptimal convergence rates with problematic extra factors: Theorem 3.5 has $(L_∞/L_∞^0)^2$ penalty; memory-efficient variant (Theorem 3.12) has dimension-dependent $d^2$ factor making it impractical in high dimensions

Weak empirical evidence: Table 1 shows ALIAS worse than tuned SIGN-SGD (3.017 vs 2.980); modest improvements in Table 2; 1.5× speedup attribution to parameter-tuning overhead rather than algorithmic gains (Table 4 shows ALIAS Adam slower per iteration)

Stochastic analysis converges only to neighborhood (Theorem 3.9); optimal rate requires increasing mini-batches (Remark 3.10) but practical experiments don't use this, creating theory-practice mismatch

Remaining hidden hyperparameters despite 'parameter-free' claims: initial approximation $d^0$, lower bound $\tilde{f}_e$ on $f(x^*)$, and $γ_t$ in momentum version; undermines core contribution framing
Limited technical novelty: per-iteration adaptive stepsizes and gradient-based smoothness estimation are incremental extensions of AdaGrad-Norm and online learning techniques

Algorithm 2 asymmetry not well-motivated: uses next step's gradient dot product with current step direction; practical vs theoretical versions differ substantially with unclear correspondence to experiments
Memory-efficient approximation is crude: replaces $\|∇f(x^t) - ∇f(x^{t-1})\|_∞$ with max/min heuristic; Figure 3 shows ~50% deviation; approximation quality not theoretically analyzed
Recent parameter-free baselines (DOG, D-ADAPTATION, MOMO) relegated to appendix Table 7, showing competitive but not superior performance; should inform main narrative
